## In one sentence

Ecological evidence connects a measured pattern to a process while accounting
for sampling, comparison, and uncertainty.

## Observation and experiment

An observation describes what occurs in nature. An experiment changes a factor
and compares the result with a control or reference condition. Observational
studies are often essential when manipulation is impossible, but confounding
factors make causal conclusions harder.

A useful question is: what would we expect to see if the proposed mechanism were
true, and what alternative mechanism predicts the same pattern?

## Sampling basics

Define the population of interest before sampling. Random or systematic
selection helps avoid choosing only convenient sites. Replication estimates
variation; repeated measurements of the same unit are not independent
replicates. Stratifying by habitat, season, or other known groups can improve
coverage.

::: {.callout-important}
Pseudoreplication occurs when several measurements from one experimental unit are
treated as independent units. The experimental unit is the smallest unit that
could have received a different treatment.
:::

## Uncertainty

A sample statistic is an estimate, not the whole population. Report the sample
size, sampling design, variability, and a measure of uncertainty such as a
confidence interval. Statistical significance does not automatically imply a
large or ecologically important effect.

## Check your understanding

Design a study testing whether mowing changes plant richness. Identify the
experimental unit, treatment, response variable, replication, and one likely
confounder.
